haiku-low.q1: On-call runs the failover command targeting B after external probes page them. Detecting A is down does nothing automatically; nothing fails over on its own.
haiku-low.q2: Step 3 stops the run, shows the lag, and releases the lock. It proceeds only if on-call reruns with the accept-data-loss override, or aborts.
haiku-low.q3: Before promotion: lock taken, A fenced (active_region=B, then 20 s wait), and lag checked or overridden. Before B's workers start: promotion done and A's running jobs requeued. Before DNS: B passes health checks.
haiku-low.q4: Nothing is carried over. B's Redis holds no sessions from A, so every user must sign in again.
haiku-low.q5: It is snapshotted so lost writes can be reviewed, then wiped and rebuilt as B's replica from a base backup. No automatic failback; returning to A is a separate planned switchover.
haiku-low.q6: A's own instances self-fence: they read active_region every 5 s and stop writing without a successful read naming A within 15 s. The privilege revoke is only a backstop.
haiku-low.q7: The control store, a 3-node strongly consistent key-value cluster with nodes in A, B and C. Only the failover command writes it; all app instances and workers in both regions read active_region.
haiku-low.q8: Step 5 sets them back to queued in B's database. B's workers rerun them after step 6, which is safe because every job is idempotent, keyed by job id.
haiku-low.q9: Rerun the command: it takes the lock and resumes at the first step not logged done, repeating any started but unfinished step. Going back to A via abort is possible only before step 4 is logged as started.
haiku-low.q10: Until DNS cache expires, up to 60 s after step 8, requests still reach A. If A is up, reads are stale and writes get 503; if A is down they fail. After the TTL, clients reach B.
haiku-low.q11: Only commits A made that B never received. If A failed outright, no more than B's recorded lag, held to 30 s unless overridden. If A was partitioned but running, commits up to 20 s after step 2 are also lost.

sonnet.q1: On-call starts it by running the failover command (target B). Detection (2 of 3 probe locations see 3 consecutive /healthz failures) only pages on-call; nothing fails over automatically.
sonnet.q2: If B's recorded lag is over 30 s (step 3), it stops, shows the lag, and releases the lock. On-call then either reruns with the accept-data-loss override (continues to promotion) or aborts (active_region back to A, A's write privileges restored, log closed). Nothing can write meanwhile.
sonnet.q3: Before promotion: the lock is taken, A is fenced (active_region = B, best-effort privilege revoke, 20 s wait), and the lag check passed or was overridden. Before B's workers start: promotion (step 4) and the requeue of running jobs (step 5) are done. Before DNS: B is scaled (step 6) and passes /healthz at its load balancer and from the probes (step 7).
sonnet.q4: B's Redis holds no sessions from A (Redis is not replicated), so every user must sign in again. This is accepted.
sonnet.q5: There is no automatic failback. A's old database is snapshotted so the lost writes can be reviewed, then wiped and rebuilt from a base backup of B as B's replica. Moving back to A is a separate, planned switchover.
sonnet.q6: The self-fencing rule. A's instances and workers read active_region every 5 s and may write only if a successful read within the last 15 s named their own region. Once active_region = B, or A loses the control store (it needs a majority, so a cut-off A cannot read it), A goes read-only. Write transactions are capped at 5 s, so A stops committing within 20 s. The privilege revoke is only a backstop.
sonnet.q7: The control store, a 3-node strongly consistent key-value cluster with one node each in A, B and C. It holds active_region, failover_lock and failover_log. Only the failover command, including its abort, writes to it. Every app instance and worker in both regions reads active_region every 5 s.
sonnet.q8: In step 5, before any B worker starts, the jobs that A's workers had marked running in B's database are set back to queued. B's workers rerun them after step 6. Jobs that A finished in its last unreplicated seconds also rerun. Jobs must be idempotent, keyed by job id.
sonnet.q9: Rerun the failover command. It takes the lock (a crashed run's lease expires within 30 s) and resumes at the first step not logged done, repeating any step that was started but not finished. Steps are safe to repeat. The team can go back to A with `failover --abort` only until step 4 (promotion) is logged as started. After that abort is refused, even after a crash mid-promotion, and the run only goes forward.
sonnet.q10: From step 2 until the cached DNS expires (up to 60 s after step 8), its requests still go to A. If A is up, its instances are self-fenced: reads work but come from A's stale database, and writes get a 503 "read-only, retry shortly". If A is down, the requests fail. After the TTL expires, the client reaches B.
sonnet.q11: Anything A committed that B never received, since replication is asynchronous. If A failed outright, the loss is at most B's recorded lag, which step 3 holds to 30 s unless on-call uses the override. If A kept running after B stopped receiving from it (a partition), A's commits up to 20 s after step 2 are also lost, and step 3 cannot see them. They survive only in A's snapshotted old database.
